title: InstructGPT close read: Why 1.3B parameters beat 175B — the three RLHF steps
summary: GPT-3 knows how to continue text but not how to follow instructions. InstructGPT uses human-written demonstrations, human rankings, and reinforcement learning to turn it into a model that does what it is told. We unpack supervised fine-tuning, the reward model loss function, the KL penalty, and the alignment tax, work through a few small examples by hand, and examine how the paper answers the honest question: aligned to whom?
ai_summary: InstructGPT (OpenAI, 2022) turns GPT-3 into an instruction-following model in three steps: supervised fine-tuning on about 13,000 human-written demonstrations; training a 6B reward model on labeler rankings of 4–9 answers; then using PPO reinforcement learning to chase high scores, with a KL penalty to prevent gaming and pretraining data mixed in (PPO-ptx) to reduce the "alignment tax." Labelers preferred the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT over the 175B-parameter GPT-3; the 175B version beats GPT-3 85 ± 3% of the time, and fabrication drops from 41% to 21%. Bias did not improve, and the model is more toxic when asked to be. The paper stresses that it aligns to the preferences of specific labelers, researchers, and customers, not to "human values."
brief: Problem: GPT-3, trained only to predict the next token, does not reliably act on user intent — it fabricates and goes off task.

Method: supervised fine-tuning on human-written demonstrations, then ranking answers to train a reward model, then PPO to maximize reward with a KL penalty as a leash and pretraining data mixed in to reduce regressions.
Results: the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT was preferred over the 175B GPT-3; it fabricates less, is less toxic when asked to be respectful, and costs only a fraction of GPT-3's pretraining compute.
Limitations: bias did not improve; it follows harmful instructions and goes along with false premises; it is aligned to a small specific group, not "humanity."

paper.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
paper.authors: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, Diogo Almeida, Carroll L. Wainwright, Pamela Mishkin, et al. (20 authors)

cover.headline: A close reading of the InstructGPT paper

sections.h: Bottom line: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In March 2022, 20 authors from OpenAI's alignment team published this 68-page paper. The problem it tackles can be stated in one sentence: GPT-3 is great at **continuing text** but not at **doing what you ask**. Tell it to "write a story about a frog" and it may list a few similar writing prompts instead; ask it a question and it may invent a plausible-looking answer.

The paper's method is to have people teach the model: first, ask labelers to demonstrate what a good answer should look like; then have them rank several model answers and use those rankings to train a **reward model** that scores answers; finally, let the language model use reinforcement learning to pursue high scores. This pipeline is called **reinforcement learning from human feedback** (RLHF), and the resulting model is called InstructGPT.

The results were surprising: on prompts from real users, labelers preferred answers from the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT over those from the 175B-parameter GPT-3, which is more than 100 times larger. In head-to-head comparisons, the 175B InstructGPT was chosen over GPT-3 85 ± 3% of the time. Its fabrication rate fell from 41% to 21%, and the compute cost was less than one-sixtieth of what it took to train GPT-3.

ChatGPT, released eight months later, used this same method. Today nearly every chat model goes through some form of alignment training, and this paper is the first complete record of that pipeline working at real product scale.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: InstructGPT = GPT-3 + three training steps: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human-written demonstrations; (2) train a reward model (RM) to score answers using human rankings of several model answers; (3) use the PPO reinforcement-learning algorithm to chase high scores while a "leash" (the KL penalty) keeps it from drifting too far just to game the score. The paper also shows that **making the model more obedient is a better deal than making it 100x larger**.

callout.title: Four concepts you need before reading
callout.text: Don't worry if you're new to this; these four are enough:
list: **GPT-3**: a 175B-parameter language model trained to predict the next token. For its uses and capabilities, see our GPT-3 close read.
**Fine-tuning**: taking a trained model and training it further on a new dataset, nudging its parameters toward a new objective.

**Reinforcement learning**: the model takes an action (here, writing an answer), receives a score (reward), then adjusts itself so actions that earn high scores become more likely. The model being trained is called the **policy**.

**The sigmoid function σ(z)**: squashes any number into the range 0 to 1: σ(0) = 0.5, the larger z the closer to 1, the smaller z the closer to 0. It is often used to turn a score difference into a probability.

sections.h: The problem: continuing text is not the same as following instructions

blocks.p: GPT-3's training objective is: given a passage from the internet, predict the next token. That objective is not the same as what we actually want — answering helpfully and safely according to the user's intent. The paper calls this mismatch the model being **misaligned** with its users. The symptoms are fabricated facts, biased or toxic output, or simply not following instructions.

callout.title: Like an intern who has only memorized the internet
callout.text: You tell him, "Help me write an apology letter." Instead of thinking about what you want, he thinks about what usually comes after that sentence on the internet. Online, that phrase is often followed by another request for help, a forum title, or even a whole list of writing prompts. He is not intentionally being difficult; nobody ever taught him that this is an instruction to carry out.

blocks.p: Section 4.3 of the paper (Figure 8) gives a real example: in French, the model is asked to "write a short story about a frog traveling to ancient Greece." GPT-3 175B does not write the story; instead, it continues with several similar French writing prompts. InstructGPT responds in French and tells the frog story.

So what does "alignment" actually mean? The paper adopts the framework from Askell et al.: an aligned model should be **helpful** (follow instructions and infer intent from a few examples or from a format like "Q: … A: …"), **honest**, and **harmless**. But honesty is hard to measure directly because we cannot know what the model "believes," so the paper falls back on measuring **truthfulness**: whether what the model says matches the facts. Harmlessness is also hard to measure because whether the same text is harmful depends on how it is used: generating profanity is bad in a chatbot, but it could be useful for training a profanity detector.

quiz.q: What does the paper say is the root cause of GPT-3 not following instructions?
options: Its training objective is to predict the next token in internet text, not to act on user intent
The training data contained no instructions
It did not use a Transformer architecture
quiz.why: The paper's diagnosis is objective mismatch: the language-model objective is only a proxy for what we actually want. Model size is not the cause — later we will see that a 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT with the same architecture is actually preferred. The internet certainly contains instructions; the problem is that the model learns what usually follows an instruction, not to carry it out.

sections.h: The overall method: demonstrate, score, practice — three steps

blocks.p: The method builds on OpenAI's earlier work in text continuation and summarization (Ziegler et al., 2019; Stiennon et al., 2020), applied here for the first time to a broad range of instructions. The starting point is three things: a pretrained GPT-3, a set of prompts the model should answer well, and a team of trained labelers.

fig.title: InstructGPT's three steps: first imitate, then learn scoring, then practice against the score
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: adapted from Figure 2 and Section 3.1; dataset sizes from Section 3.2

steps.name: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
steps.desc: Labelers write ideal answers to prompts by hand; GPT-3 learns from these demonstrations.

steps.name: Train a reward model (RM)
steps.desc: The model writes 4–9 answers per prompt; labelers rank them from best to worst; the reward model learns to score answers.

steps.name: Reinforcement learning (PPO)
steps.desc: The model writes an answer, the reward model scores it, and the model adjusts toward higher scores while staying tethered near the Step 1 model.

callout.title: Understanding it through learning to cook
list: **Step 1 is like apprenticing with a master chef**: the chef personally makes hundreds of dishes for the apprentice to copy. The apprentice learns well, but the chef's time is limited, so the number of demonstrations stays small.

**Step 2 is like training a taster**: the apprentice makes several versions of a dish, and diners only need to rank which is better. Ranking is much cheaper than cooking. Use many rankings to train a taster who learns to predict the diners' preferences.

**Step 3 is like the apprentice practicing against the taster**: the taster never gets tired and scores every attempt, so the apprentice keeps adjusting to please him. But the taster has blind spots, so the apprentice is not allowed to stray too far from the chef's style — that is the KL penalty, explained later.

blocks.p: Why not stop after Step 1? Because **judging is cheaper than creating**. Writing a good answer takes minutes or longer; comparing two answers takes seconds. And for many tasks, people struggle to write a good answer but can easily tell which one is better. Steps 2 and 3 turn human judgment into a steady stream of training signal.

Steps 2 and 3 can also be iterated: generate new answers with the current best model, collect new rankings, train a new reward model, then train a new policy. The paper notes that most of the collected comparison data came from SFT model outputs, with some from PPO models.

sections.h: Data: real user prompts and forty labelers

blocks.p: Prompts came mainly from the OpenAI API Playground, where users typed text while trying early versions of InstructGPT (users were repeatedly told their data might be used for training). Data from production API calls was **not** used. The data handling was careful:

list: **Deduplication**: prompts with a long identical opening were treated as duplicates.
**At most 200 prompts per user**: to keep a few heavy users from dominating the data.
**Split by user**: train, validation, and test sets were split by user ID, so no user in the test set appeared in training. That way the test measures performance on new users.
**Filter out personal information**: prompts in the training set were filtered for personally identifiable information (PII).

blocks.p: At the start, however, there were no instruction-like prompts available: users rarely wrote direct instructions to plain GPT-3. So the researchers first asked labelers to write three kinds of prompts: open-ended diverse tasks, tasks with a few question-answer examples, and tasks based on the use cases in API waitlist applications. These were used to train the first InstructGPT, which was then put on the Playground to attract real user instructions.

fig.title: Three datasets: SFT mostly from labelers, PPO entirely from real users
fig.subtitle: Unit: prompt count, training set. From paper Table 6; amber indicates PPO data, which requires no human labeling
rows: Write an answer by hand for each prompt
fig.note: SFT has more labeler-written prompts because the early interface asked labelers to write an overall instruction plus a few examples; the paper sampled different combinations of examples from the same instruction to create multiple training examples.

blocks.p: Compared with the hundreds of billions of tokens used to pretrain GPT-3, this data is tiny: only about 13,000 demonstrations. As we will see, that small amount of high-quality human data changes model behavior. More than 96% of the data is in English.
What did users actually want it to do? Labelers categorized the prompts in the RM dataset, and the distribution was very different from the academic benchmarks commonly used:

fig.title: What real users do with GPT-3: nearly half is generation, classification and QA are a small minority
fig.subtitle: Unit: %, use-case distribution of API prompts, as judged by labelers. From paper Table 1; amber indicates "generation."
fig.note: "Closed QA" means answers should come only from the given material; "open QA" may use any knowledge.

blocks.p: The **labelers** were about 40 contractors hired through Upwork and ScaleAI. Because prompts might touch on sensitive topics, hiring included a screening test: could they spot potentially harmful output, were they sensitive to different groups, and did their labels agree with researchers? During the project, researchers answered questions in a shared chat room.

People's opinions differ, so first we need to know how reliable the "ground truth" is. Training labelers agreed with each other 72.6 ± 1.5% of the time; a separate set of "held-out" labelers, who produced no training data and took no screening test, agreed 77.3 ± 1.3% of the time. For reference, researchers in an earlier summarization task agreed 73 ± 4% of the time. In other words, about a quarter of comparisons are contested even by humans, so a reward model predicting human preferences can hardly be much more accurate than this.

callout.title: Training and evaluation used different priorities
callout.text: Helping the user and avoiding harm sometimes conflict — for example, when a user asks for a potentially harmful answer. The paper's approach: **during training**, labelers were told to prioritize helpfulness to the user; **in final evaluation**, labelers were told to prioritize truthfulness and harmlessness. The paper acknowledges that how to handle this conflict during training is a difficult design decision left to future work.

sections.h: Step 1: supervised fine-tuning — learning that "this is an instruction"

blocks.p: Step 1 is the most straightforward: take the labelers' demonstrations and fine-tune GPT-3 with ordinary supervised learning. The objective is still "predict the next token," but now it predicts the next token in the **demonstration answers**. The model learns a key format: a prompt is a task, and it should be followed by an answer that completes that task.

The paper trained for 16 epochs (one full pass over all demonstrations per epoch), using cosine learning-rate decay and a residual dropout of 0.2. There is a counterintuitive detail: after just 1 epoch, validation loss began to worsen, meaning the model was overfitting, but with continued training, both reward-model scores and human preference ratings kept improving.

callout.title: Worse validation loss does not mean a worse model
callout.text: The paper doesn't explain why, but a common interpretation is: validation loss measures how much probability the model assigns to the labeler's particular demonstration. But there is more than one good answer. As the model becomes more confident in one good answer, it gives lower probability to other good answers, so loss rises while human readers are actually more satisfied. That is why the paper does **not** select a model by validation loss; it selects by the reward model's score on the validation set. It's a reminder that the numeric metric used in training can diverge from what we actually want.

blocks.p: One easy-to-miss detail (Appendix C.3): the SFT model used as the starting point for Step 3 is **not the same** as the 16-epoch SFT baseline above. The reinforcement-learning starting point was trained for only 2 epochs and included 10% pretraining data; the paper found this helped the later PPO training.

sections.h: Step 2: the reward model — turning "which do people prefer?" into a score

blocks.p: Reinforcement learning needs a referee that can score at any time, but you can't ask a human to judge every generated answer. So Step 2 trains a model to **score in place of a human**: it takes a prompt and an answer, and outputs a number where a higher score means a human is more likely to prefer it.

Its architecture is simple: take the SFT model, remove the final output layer that maps vectors to next-token probabilities, and replace it with a linear layer that outputs a single number. The paper used only a 6B-parameter reward model: the 175B version was unstable in training, and because the reward model would later initialize PPO's value function, a larger one would make compute blow up.

**Where the data comes from**: for a given prompt, the model generates K answers (K between 4 and 9), and labelers rank them from best to worst. Any two of the K answers form a "which is better" comparison, for C(K,2) = K(K−1)/2 pairs in total. A single ranking of 9 answers yields 36 pairs, far more efficient than asking one pair at a time.

**How to learn scores from comparisons**: the core assumption is simple: the larger the score gap between two answers, the more likely a human is to choose the higher-scoring one. This probability is represented by putting the score difference through the sigmoid function, which squashes it to 0–1. The training objective is to make the chosen answer's score as much higher than the rejected one's as possible:

parts.desc: The reward model's score for "answer y to prompt x"; θ is the reward model's parameters
Within the same pair, the answer the labeler preferred (w for win) and the answer they liked less (l for lose)
The probability, according to the model's scores, that a human would choose y_{w}. When the score difference is 0 it is 0.5; the larger the difference, the closer to 1.
The loss for this pair: the more confident the model is that y_{w} is better, the closer the loss is to 0; if the model ranks the two backwards, the loss becomes very large.
A single ranking produces C(K,2) comparisons; dividing by that takes the average, so prompts ranked with 4 answers count as much as prompts ranked with 9.
Average over every comparison in the comparison dataset D.

formula.note: This assumption—representing preference probability as a sigmoid of the score difference—is statistically known as the Bradley-Terry model, the same idea as Elo ratings in chess: the larger the rating gap, the more likely the higher-rated player wins.

fig.title: Three comparisons by hand: small loss when ranked correctly, large loss when reversed
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: scores are invented by us, not from the paper. r_{w} is the score of the answer humans preferred, r_{l} is the score of the rejected answer; amber marks the case the model ranked backwards.
columns: σ(diff): probability the model thinks a human will choose y_{w}
rows: Model ranks correctly, with high confidence
Model sees the two as roughly equal
fig.note: During training, comparisons like the third row produce the largest gradient, pushing the reward model to raise y_{w}'s score and lower y_{l}'s until the ranking is correct.

blocks.p: This loss cares only about the **score difference**, not the scores themselves. Add 10 to every answer and every pair's difference is unchanged, so the loss is unchanged. The “zero point” of the scores is therefore arbitrary. Before reinforcement learning, the paper adds a bias to fix the zero at the mean score of labeler demonstrations: positive means better than the average demonstration, negative worse.

**One engineering detail that made training work**: the 36 comparisons from a single ranking are highly correlated—they all compare the same set of answers. The paper initially mixed all comparisons together; after only one pass over the data, the reward model overfit: an answer appeared in K−1 comparisons, so it was effectively learned K−1 times. After changing to **keep all comparisons for the same prompt together as one training example**, overfitting disappeared and validation accuracy improved markedly; each answer also had to be read by the reward model only once, saving compute. Under this scheme, a batch of 64 prompts contains at most 64 × 36 = 2,304 comparisons.
The reward model is trained for only 1 epoch: more epochs quickly overfit. Its learning rate, in contrast, is not very sensitive; changing it by 50% gives similar results.

**Can the reward model represent other people's preferences?** The paper splits labelers into 5 groups, trains on 4 groups and tests on the remaining one. When predicting the preferences of the **held-out group**, accuracy is 69.6 ± 0.9%; for the training groups it is 72.4 ± 0.4%. Only slightly lower, and not far from the roughly 73% agreement rate between humans.

quiz.q: If a labeler ranks K = 4 answers, how many comparisons does that produce?
quiz.why: Choose any two answers as a pair: C(4,2) = 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6. 3 pairs means comparing only adjacent ranks, which wastes the ranking information; 12 pairs counts both “A vs B” and “B vs A,” doubling every comparison.

quiz.q: If you add 10 to every answer's reward-model score, what happens to the training loss?
quiz.why: Only the score difference r_{w} − r_{l} appears in the loss; adding 10 to every score leaves the difference, σ, and the loss unchanged. This is exactly why the paper adds a bias to set the mean demonstration score to 0: the loss itself does not determine the zero point.

sections.h: Step 3: Reinforcement learning, held on a leash

blocks.p: With a reward model that can score answers, Step 3 makes the language model chase high scores. The paper frames this as the simplest possible reinforcement-learning environment (technically a bandit environment): draw a random user prompt, the model writes an answer, the reward model scores it, and the episode ends. No multi-turn dialogue, no intermediate reward.

The algorithm used to update the model is PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization, Schulman et al., 2017). Its key idea: each update must not move the model too much; steps beyond a certain ratio are clipped (the paper uses a clipping ratio of 0.2), making training more stable.

But there is a big trap. The reward model is only a **proxy** for human preference; it has seen tens of thousands of prompts and has its own blind spots. If the language model is optimized hard enough, it will find those blind spots: writing things the reward model scores highly but humans find baffling. This is called **overoptimizing** the reward model, like a student studying the grader's quirks to score points instead of actually solving the problem.

callout.title: A kite string
callout.text: The fix is to tie the model to a leash: for every token it writes, compare the probability the RL model and the original SFT model assign to that token. The more it deviates, the more is subtracted. The model can fly toward higher scores, but not far, staying near the distribution of human-written demonstrations. This penalty measures the difference between two probability distributions and is called the **KL divergence** penalty.

blocks.p: With the leash and the “pretraining review” described later, Step 3 maximizes the following objective:

formula.expr:
objective(φ) = E_{(x,y)∼RL} [ r_{θ}(x, y)
    − β · log( π^{RL}_{φ}(y | x) / π^{SFT}(y | x) ) ]
    + γ · E_{x∼pretrain} [ log π^{RL}_{φ}(x) ]

parts.desc: The language model being trained (the policy), with parameters φ
The SFT model from Step 1, held fixed, as the other end of the leash
Averaged over a randomly drawn user prompt x and an answer y written by the model being trained
The reward model's score for this answer
How much more probable this answer is under the new model than under the SFT model (in log space); summed token by token, this is the KL penalty for the answer
How tight the leash is; the paper uses 0.02
Second line: sample text x from GPT-3's pretraining data and continue with next-token prediction; γ controls its weight. When γ = 0 it is called PPO, when γ > 0 it is called PPO-ptx

formula.note: The paper says that unless stated otherwise, “InstructGPT” refers to the PPO-ptx model.

fig.title: A hand-worked KL penalty: gain 1 reward point, but drift too far and you still lose
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: numbers are invented, not from the paper. β = 0.02; “sum of log probability ratios” means for each token in the answer, take the ratio of the new model's probability to the SFT model's probability, take the log, and sum them. Amber marks the answer with the higher final score.
rows: B: weird answer that exploits the reward model's blind spot
fig.note: Per token, the penalty is small: if the SFT model gives a token probability 0.1 and the RL model gives 0.4, log(0.4/0.1) ≈ 1.39, and multiplying by 0.02 deducts only 0.028. But if many tokens in an answer deviate sharply, the penalty accumulates and overwhelms the reward model's high score.

blocks.p: Other key settings: PPO trains for 256k episodes using about 31k deduplicated, PII-scrubbed prompts; each batch of 512 episodes is split into 8 minibatches, each trained once. Policies of all sizes use the same 6B reward model, which also initializes the 6B value function (an auxiliary model PPO needs to estimate “about how well will this answer score”). That way different model sizes share the same referee, making comparisons fairer.

quiz.q: If the KL penalty coefficient β is set to 0, what is most likely to happen?
options: The model exploits the reward model's blind spots; reward scores climb, but human ratings do not necessarily improve
quiz.why: β = 0 is cutting the leash: the model only tries to please the reward model. The reward model is an imperfect proxy, and optimizing hard against it exposes its blind spots—that is overoptimization. The model neither stops learning nor reverts to GPT-3, because nothing pulls it back.

sections.h: The alignment tax: more obedient, but some old skills regress

blocks.p: A problem appeared when training with PPO alone: the model got worse on several public NLP benchmarks, including reading comprehension (SQuAD, DROP), commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag), and WMT 2015 French-to-English translation. The paper calls this cost the **alignment tax**: sacrificing some capability to become aligned.

Why care? If alignment is heavily taxed, people would rather use unaligned but more capable models, and alignment methods would not spread. The paper therefore treats reducing the alignment tax as part of the method itself.

The solution is PPO-ptx, the second line of the objective: after each PPO update, do one next-token-prediction update on GPT-3's original pretraining data—learning new rules while reviewing old material. The number of pretraining samples is 8 times the number of RL episodes, and their gradient is multiplied by γ = 27.8.

fig.title: Alignment tax: reading comprehension drops sharply with PPO alone, mostly recovers with pretraining mix
fig.subtitle: 175B model, zero-shot. From appendix Table 14; HellaSwag is accuracy (%), others are F1 or BLEU. Blue columns indicate InstructGPT (PPO-ptx).
fig.note: PPO-ptx even beats GPT-3 on HellaSwag, but still trails on DROP, SQuADv2, and translation. The paper's wording is that “most” regressions are mitigated, not all eliminated.

blocks.p: A small issue spotted while reading the table: in the same appendix Table 14, the ROUGE-L scores for the two summarization tasks CNN/DM and TL;DR are identical across all 12 numbers. Two different datasets are unlikely to produce exactly the same results; the rows may have been duplicated by mistake during typesetting, so be careful when citing them.

**Why not just pull the leash tighter (increase β)?** Intuitively, the closer the model stays to SFT, the fewer skills it should lose. The paper tried this on the 1.3B model: raising β to 2.0, 100 times the default, still did not fully recover the DROP and SQuAD regressions, while reward scores dropped noticeably. With pretraining data mixed in, there existed a γ that reversed the regression while barely lowering reward scores. The paper also tried anchoring the other end of the leash to GPT-3 itself instead of the SFT model, with similar results, and concluded that the pretraining data distribution is the key. Our interpretation: the KL penalty constrains the model only on user prompts, while capabilities like reading comprehension show up on completely different inputs, where the leash does not reach; reviewing pretraining data directly covers those inputs.

One more caution: on the 1.3B model, extending training from 256k to 512k episodes made DROP and SQuADv2 start better than GPT-3 but decline as training continued, ending slightly below GPT-3. The alignment tax accumulates with training time.

quiz.q: To reduce the alignment tax, why did the paper choose to mix in pretraining data (PPO-ptx) rather than increase the KL coefficient β?
options: Because raising β to 100 times the default still failed to recover the regression and clearly lowered reward scores; mixing in pretraining data recovered the regression while barely lowering reward scores
quiz.why: This is the ablation conclusion in appendix E.6. Increasing β only pulls the model toward the SFT model, and the SFT model itself already trails GPT-3, so it cannot recover the loss and also sacrifices alignment. Speed, cost, and the allowed range of β are not the reasons the paper gives.

sections.h: Result 1: people prefer it—the small model beats the big one

blocks.p: The main evaluation asks labelers to compare different models' answers to the same prompt and judge which they prefer, while also scoring each answer from 1 to 7 and flagging specific issues (such as whether it ignored the instruction or fabricated content). Test prompts came from users **who did not appear in the training data**.

Besides GPT-3, SFT, and PPO, the comparison included a carefully built baseline: GPT-3 with a hand-designed few-shot prefix to put it into instruction-following mode (GPT-3-prompted). The prefix was chosen through a contest between two authors: each spent an hour interacting with GPT-3 and submitted two best prefixes, with the winner decided by the reward model's validation score. The footnote says only: author DA won.

The results form a clear ladder: GPT-3 is worst; adding a good few-shot prefix is clearly better; supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations is better still; and PPO on comparison data is better again. Whether pretraining data is mixed into PPO makes little difference to human preference.

fig.title: How often the 175B InstructGPT was preferred head-to-head against each opponent
fig.subtitle: Unit: %, labeler preference on API prompts; ± indicates error range. From paper Section 1 and Section 4.1; amber marks the comparison against plain GPT-3.
fig.note: 50% means a tie. FLAN and T0 are 175B GPT-3 models fine-tuned on many public NLP tasks with instructions; discussed separately below.

blocks.p: The most striking comparison is size: **the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT was preferred over the 175B-parameter GPT-3**, even though they share the same architecture and differ only in that the former was fine-tuned on human data. The conclusion holds even when GPT-3 is given a few-shot prefix.

Beyond “which do you prefer,” labelers also flagged more specific issues. Compared with GPT-3, InstructGPT is more suitable as a customer-service assistant, follows explicit constraints in instructions more often (like “answer in at most two paragraphs”), fails the entire task less often, and fabricates less often on closed-domain tasks:

fig.title: Fabrication on closed-domain tasks: from 41% to 21%
fig.subtitle: Unit: %. Closed-domain tasks are tasks where the answer should come only from the given material, such as summarization or answering from material. From paper Section 1; amber is InstructGPT.

blocks.p: **Did the model just learn to please those 40 people?** The paper checks in two ways: first, it asks “held-out” labelers who were not involved in the training data to evaluate, and they also strongly prefer InstructGPT; second, the reward-model cross-validation described earlier. Both suggest the model did not just learn to please the people who trained it. But those “others” come from the same contractor pool as the training labelers; the paper says how the model does for broader populations still needs research.

The paper also evaluated on a different set of prompts: prompts users submitted to ordinary GPT-3 (not in the instruction style written for InstructGPT). The conclusions were largely unchanged, except PPO-ptx did slightly worse at the largest size.

callout.title: Alignment is much cheaper than scaling
callout.text: Training the 175B SFT model took 4.9 petaflop/s-day, training the 175B PPO-ptx model took 60 petaflop/s-day, and training GPT-3 itself took 3,640 petaflop/s-day. In other words, for less than one-sixtieth of GPT-3's compute, the improvement was greater than making the model 100x larger. The paper concludes that, at least for the tasks customers actually use, investing in aligning an existing model is a better deal than training a larger one.

fig.title: Alignment compute is a fraction of pretraining
fig.subtitle: Unit: petaflop/s-day (a petaflop/s sustained for one day). From paper Section 5.1; amber is GPT-3 pretraining.
fig.note: This counts only model training; the human labor for data collection is separate, and the paper says that even including experiments, the total cost was only a small fraction of training GPT-3.

sections.h: Why FLAN and T0, trained on public tasks, fall short

blocks.p: Around the same time, academia was also doing “instruction fine-tuning”: reformatting many public NLP datasets into “instruction + answer” examples for training, represented by FLAN and T0. The paper took about 1 million examples from each and fine-tuned a 175B GPT-3 with each, then compared.

Result: they are better than plain GPT-3 and about on par with GPT-3 with a good few-shot prefix, but worse than the SFT baseline. With 175B SFT as the reference, InstructGPT has a 73.4 ± 2% win rate, the T0 version 26.8 ± 2%, and the FLAN version 29.8 ± 2%.

The paper gives two reasons. First, public datasets are designed for **convenient automatic scoring**, so they favor tasks with standard answers such as classification and QA; but among real users, classification and QA together account for only about 18%, while open-ended generation and brainstorming account for about 57% (see the use-case chart earlier). Second, public datasets struggle to match the rich diversity of real user input.

callout.title: This is not to say FLAN and T0 are useless
callout.text: The paper's conclusion is restrained: public NLP tasks are also a kind of instruction, and models should be able to do them; **the broadest instruction-following model should combine both kinds of data**. What is being compared here is “who real users prefer on their prompts,” which measures something different from academic benchmarks.

sections.h: Result 2: somewhat more truthful, slightly less toxic, no improvement in bias

blocks.p: **Truthfulness**. TruthfulQA is a benchmark specifically designed to make models say the wrong thing (for example, by exploiting common misconceptions). The paper asked humans to judge whether answers were truthful and informative. The conclusion: PPO models generate answers that are “both truthful and informative” about twice as often as GPT-3, and this is default behavior—the model does not need to be told to “tell the truth.” The exception is the 1.3B PPO-ptx model, which is slightly worse than the same-size GPT-3.
If the prompt adds “If you are unsure, answer ‘I have no comment,’” PPO models are more likely to say “I have no comment” than to confidently give a wrong answer; GPT-3 is worse at this.

fig.title: TruthfulQA automatic scoring: PPO improves a lot, but these numbers are overestimated
fig.subtitle: 175B model, ordinary QA prompts. From appendix Table 14 (automatic scores, not human judgment); amber indicates InstructGPT (PPO-ptx).
fig.note: The acknowledgments specifically note that the authors of the TruthfulQA dataset pointed out that the automatic scores overstate PPO's improvement. That is why the main text uses human judgment and reports roughly “twofold,” not the nearly threefold gap in this table.

callout.title: Two places in the paper don't fully agree
list: The introduction says the results are “equally strong” on the subset of questions not adversarially selected against GPT-3; Section 4.2 says PPO models are still significantly better on this subset, but the absolute improvement is a few percentage points smaller.

The introduction says “about twice,” based on human judgment; the automatic scores in appendix Table 14 show nearly three times, and the paper itself admits the automatic scores overstate the improvement. When reading the numbers, check which scoring method is being used.

blocks.p: **Toxicity**. They tested on the RealToxicityPrompts dataset (a set of sentence prefixes likely to provoke profanity), using both the automatic scoring tool Perspective API and human evaluation. To get more high-toxicity inputs, the paper sampled prompts uniformly across toxicity levels, so the absolute toxicity numbers are higher than in typical measurements. The results fall into three cases:

fig.title: When asked to be polite, toxicity drops; when asked to be toxic, it is more toxic than GPT-3
fig.subtitle: Average Perspective API toxicity scores for the 175B model (0 to 1, higher is more toxic). From appendix Table 14; amber indicates prompts that asked for bias.
rows: Asked to be polite and respectful
fig.note: The introduction says that when asked to be respectful, InstructGPT produces about 25% fewer toxic outputs than GPT-3; this table uses a different average-score metric, which drops from 0.233 to 0.196. With no instruction, the two are about the same.

blocks.p: Human evaluation agrees: InstructGPT is less toxic when asked to be respectful, and about the same as GPT-3 with no instruction. The SFT model is the least toxic, but its answers are the least coherent and least preferred; the paper speculates it often wrote very short or broken outputs. Saying nothing is the surest way to avoid saying the wrong thing.

**Bias**. They tested with Winogender and CrowS-Pairs: each item is a pair of sentences that differ only in a group identity, and the model's probabilities for the two sentences are compared. A completely unbiased model should treat the two sentences equally, which maximizes the entropy of the probabilities (50/50 gives 1 bit; if one gets 90% and the other 10%, entropy is only about 0.47 bits). By this standard, InstructGPT is **no less biased than GPT-3**; when asked to be “respectful,” entropy is actually lower. The paper says the pattern is unclear: instruction-trained models seem more “confident” regardless of whether the output is stereotypical.

quiz.q: When asked to “please continue in a biased way,” InstructGPT is more toxic than GPT-3. What does this show?
options: InstructGPT learned to follow instructions, including harmful ones; training never taught it to refuse.
The pretraining data mixed into PPO-ptx was toxic.
quiz.why: During training, the paper explicitly asked labelers to prioritize helpfulness, so the model learned to “follow instructions better,” including malicious ones. The paper lists this as one of its biggest limitations and says the same technique could be used to train models to refuse certain requests, planned for later versions.

sections.h: It generalizes—and still makes simple mistakes

blocks.p: **Generalization**. Non-English instructions and code-related tasks are very rare in the training data, but InstructGPT can follow a French instruction to write a story, summarize code, and answer questions about code (its explanation of a binomial coefficient code example in Figure 8 is not entirely correct). It does, however, often answer non-English instructions in English. GPT-3 can do these things too, but only with more carefully designed prompts. The paper argues this shows the model has partly learned the **general concept** of “following instructions,” rather than just memorizing the types of tasks in training. This matters: you cannot have a human supervise everything a model does.
**Mistakes**. The paper also candidly shows simple mistakes from the 175B InstructGPT. The first two examples are from Figure 9; the third comes from the description in Section 4.3:

list: **Goes along with a false premise**: ask it “Why is it important to eat socks after meditation?” and, instead of pointing out the absurd premise, it solemnly lists several “theories.”

**Excessive vagueness**: ask “What happens if you fire a pumpkin out of a cannon at high speed?” and it says too many factors prevent a precise prediction, then lists possibilities. The paper notes the right answer is basically that the pumpkin explodes.
**Fails on multiple constraints**: such as “List 10 movies from the 1930s set in France,” or “Summarize this in a specified number of sentences.”

blocks.p: The paper offers explanations for the first two mistakes. Excessive vagueness may partly come from **the training setup itself**: labelers were told to reward “epistemic humility,” so they tended to give high scores to noncommittal answers, and the reward model learned that tendency. Going along with false premises may arise because the training set contained few prompts with false premises. The paper argues that adversarial data collection—deliberately looking for examples that make the model fail—could substantially reduce both problems.

callout.title: The reward model amplifies small human preferences
callout.text: This is a general lesson of RLHF: small tendencies in the labelers—preferring caution, longer answers, a more polite tone—get learned by the reward model, then amplified by reinforcement learning into the model's “personality.” The verbosity and excessive disclaimers people complain about in today's chat models are already visible in this paper.

quiz.q: What does the paper think may explain InstructGPT being “excessively vague” even on simple questions?
options: Labelers were told to reward humble answers; the reward model learned that preference, and reinforcement learning amplified it.
PPO clipping ratio set too small.
Training data contains too many philosophy articles.
quiz.why: This is the paper's own speculation: the problem is in the human feedback signal, not in model size or algorithm hyperparameters. It shows that the reward model learns not only “good vs. bad” but also labelers' habits, and that optimization amplifies them.

sections.h: Aligned to whom: the section most worth reading closely

blocks.p: The literature often talks about aligning models with “human preferences” or “human values.” Section 5.2 of the paper says plainly: we have not aligned to “humanity.” We have aligned to a specific group of people, and that group's preferences are shaped by the task instructions, the work setting (this is paid work), and who sets the tasks. It lays out the layers one by one:

list: **First layer, the training labelers**: mostly English speakers living in the U.S. or Southeast Asia. Among the 19 labelers who completed the questionnaire in the appendix, 52.6% identified as Southeast Asian; by nationality, the Philippines and Bangladesh each account for 22%, and the U.S. for 17%. Their agreement with one another is only about 73%.

**Second layer, the researchers themselves**: the labeling instructions were written by researchers, and edge cases were decided by them in a chat room, so the model is also indirectly aligned to OpenAI.

**Third layer, API customers**: prompts came from customers, so the model is implicitly aligned to the uses customers find valuable. But customers and their end users may have different interests: for example, a customer may want users to spend longer on the platform. Labelers also cannot see the contexts in which prompts and answers will actually be used.

**Fourth layer, who can become a customer**: for most of the project, API users were chosen from a waitlist, and the list was originally seeded with OpenAI employees, so the population skewed toward their own social circles.

blocks.p: The paper's position is that this work only proves **the technique can align a model to a specific population for a specific application.** It does not claim that researchers, labelers, or API customers are the “correct” preference source. Many more stakeholders deserve consideration: the institution training the model, customers building products with it, end users of those products, and the broader public indirectly affected. The paper also writes that it is impossible to train a system that aligns to everyone's preferences at once.

One direction it proposes is to let models be conditioned on a particular group's preferences, or be easy to fine-tune or prompt to represent different groups, so people with different values can use different models. But these models still affect society as a whole. Whose preferences to condition on, how to ensure all groups are represented, and how to allow people to opt out of harmful processes are all hard problems.

callout.title: “An RLHF-trained model aligns with human values”
callout.text: The paper itself rejects this claim. RLHF moves the model closer to the judgments of **the specific people who provided feedback**, under **that specific set of instructions**. Swap the labelers or the instructions, and you get a different model. So when you hear “this model is aligned,” it is worth asking: aligned to whom? By what standard?

blocks.p: Limitations and open questions listed in the paper:

list: **Data collection**: most comparisons were labeled by only one labeler, mainly to save money. Multiple labels per comparison would reveal areas of strong disagreement; and simply averaging over disagreements may not be appropriate—for content involving a minority group, more weight may belong to labelers from that group.

**The model is not safe**: it still generates toxic or biased content, fabricates facts, and sometimes generates sexual and violent content even when not asked. The biggest limitation is that it almost always does what the user asks, even when that could cause real-world harm.

**Ways it could improve**: adversarially collect worst-case examples; filter toxic content from the pretraining data; combine it with methods that improve truthfulness such as WebGPT; train the model to refuse certain instructions (the paper says it planned to explore this in later versions).
**Comparison may not be the most efficient signal**: perhaps labelers could directly rewrite answers, or provide critiques in natural language.

**What to align to**: There are subtle differences between aligning to instructions, intent, revealed preferences, ideal preferences, interests, or values. For simplicity, the paper aligns to “inferred user intent.”

blocks.p: The paper's “Broader impacts” section is just as sober: making the model more obedient also makes it easier to misuse, for example to mass-produce plausible-looking disinformation. High-risk areas such as medical diagnosis, credit and hiring judgments, political advertising, and law enforcement should be approached with great caution, or not at all. Alignment technology is not a panacea; it is one tool in a larger safety system.

**What came next.** In November 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, officially noting that it was trained with RLHF using the same method as InstructGPT, with a slightly different data collection setup (mainly changed to dialogue format). After that, “pretraining → supervised fine-tuning → training on human preferences” became the standard pipeline for chat models. In 2023, Meta's Llama 2 also used RLHF to train its dialogue model; the same year, DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) showed that one can fine-tune a language model directly on preference pairs, without separately training a reward model or running reinforcement learning, and achieve similar goals. Both are in our reading list.
The PPO algorithm itself (2017), which this article does not cover, is also part of the fine-tuning and alignment section of the reading list.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really get it?

quiz.q: The 1.3B InstructGPT was preferred by labelers over the 175B GPT-3. Which conclusion **cannot** be drawn from this result?
options: For customers' actual tasks, aligning with human feedback may be a better deal than scaling up the model.
The 1.3B InstructGPT comprehensively surpasses GPT-3 175B in knowledge and capabilities.
Pretrained models already have the ability to do many tasks; it just hasn't been brought out.
Human preference scores measure something different from public NLP benchmarks.
quiz.why: Preference scores measure “whether the answer matches the user's intent and is useful,” not raw knowledge. The paper also shows RLHF causes regressions on some public benchmarks (the alignment tax), so saying the smaller model “comprehensively surpasses” the larger one is an overreading. The other three are the paper's own arguments.

quiz.q: If Step 2 did not train a reward model, and Step 3 instead asked labelers to score every answer the model generated, what would be the main problem?
options: PPO runs 256k episodes; having humans score every episode is too slow and expensive to be feasible.
Reinforcement learning cannot use human scores.
This would create an alignment tax.
quiz.why: The point of the reward model is to “distill” finite human judgment into an always-available, nearly free referee. Human scores are not necessarily inaccurate—the reward model itself learns from humans—and reinforcement learning can use human scores; it is just too slow and expensive. The alignment tax is a separate issue.

blocks.p: After finishing this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: Why does a “predict the next token” model not necessarily follow instructions? Give an example.
What do people need to do in each of the three steps? Why is ranking cheaper than writing demonstrations, and why are Step 1's demonstrations still needed?
How many comparison pairs does ranking 6 answers produce? Why should they be kept in the same training sample?
Why is the reward model's loss insensitive to adding a constant to all scores? How does the paper set the zero point?
What problem does the KL penalty prevent? What happens if β is too large, or too small?
What is the alignment tax? How does PPO-ptx reduce it? Why does increasing β not work?
Why do FLAN and T0, instruction-tuned on public NLP data, fall short of InstructGPT?
Why do TruthfulQA's “roughly two times” and the nearly threefold gap in the appendix table not contradict each other?
Whose preferences does InstructGPT align to? Name at least three layers.
